I-D magazine interview (around Galore): Oklou called Arca "the REAL star of current experimental music."

Robinson, in a triple j interview with Ninajirachi, on two things he took from her into his own studio practice: her approach to lyrics -- "she would just kind of like come up with stuff and not overthink it and go for it and sell it really. MusicTech, invoking "another of her musical heroes, SOPHIE, who manipulated technology to bold and thrilling effect."

DIY Magazine (Sept 2023), naming Radiohead among a cluster of '90s and 2000s reference points.

Spin's Garrett Kamps, reviewing Worlds, "identified melodic similarities with Boards of Canada."
Wikipedia/Faust: "cited as an influence by Radiohead, Swell Maps, Throbbing Gristle, Cabaret Voltaire, Stereolab, Simple Minds, Sonic Youth, Mark E. Smith, Nurse with Wound and Madlib."

Far Out's account of Bjork's own published favourites list, which includes Aphex Twin.
Billboard reported that Bright Eyes's I'm Wide Awake, It's Morning influenced Phoebe Bridgers's song "Graceland Too."
Guitar Player wrote on Johnny Marr's folk stylings, listing Bert Jansch first among his named guitarist influences.

Robin Pecknold told Paste that Helplessness Blues "was about honoring our influences, like Roy Harper and Joanna Newsom and Joni Mitchell"; Georgia Straight and Guitar Techniques both corroborate Roy Harper shaping the album's direction.
In the same Believer interview, Joanna Newsom said she loves Karen Dalton, a sixties singer who ran with Fred Neil and Bob Dylan and had a beautiful voice.

The same rare Pitchfork interview: the duo say they are big fans of the Cocteau Twins and My Bloody Valentine.

Kurt Vile told Rolling Stone in September 2020 that he began listening to John Prine in his early twenties after a fan told him he sounded like Prine, and spent what he called "one cool summer" on the greatest hits.

Fleet Foxes named John Prine directly in their own lyrics on "Sunblind," alongside Judee Sill, Elliott Smith and David Berman; Robin Pecknold told Under the Radar the song expresses gratitude toward songwriters whose work had affected him.

Sufjan Stevens told Uncut in February 2015 that there was no music, art or television at home growing up -- his stepfather Lowell Brams introduced him and his siblings to the Beatles, the Rolling Stones, Ry Cooder, Bob Dylan, Nick Drake and Frank Zappa the summer they moved to Eugene, an experience Stevens described as Brams opening a Pandora's box.
Guitar Techniques reported that Robin Pecknold's songwriting is influenced by Bob Dylan, Neil Young and Hank Williams, and that his love of Brian Wilson is audible in Fleet Foxes' harmonies.
Riffology has written that Bob Dylan shaped Jeff Buckley's sound, pointing to Dylan covers in his live repertoire as evidence.

Justin Vernon told Pitchfork, quoted via Ewing's Voice, "after growing up in a Neil Young/Bob Dylan/Indigo Girls/John Prine subjective-songwriter kind of world, I finally realized I didn't have what they had."

AllMusic's prose biography and Wikipedia's sourced influence line describe Kurt Vile as taking notes from masters including Neil Young; Premier Guitar wrote in June 2026 that his sound draws on grunge, DIY recording, and whatever Neil Young happened to be doing at the time.
The same Guitar Techniques piece names Neil Young alongside Bob Dylan and Hank Williams as an influence on Robin Pecknold's songwriting.
Mark Kozelek told beermelodies in May 2009 that he definitely loves Neil Young, and Stereogum has called Young one of Kozelek's favorite artists, noting his eventual shift to a higher vocal register.

Mac DeMarco has described himself as an obsessive Neil Young listener who played Harvest several times a day for months, telling The Guardian he wanted his album 2 to sound "really dry, really crisp '70s style" like it; he discussed the same ambition again in a 2023 Weekly Neil interview, recalling recording it broke in Montreal and digging through a thrift-store dollar bin.

The same Pitchfork quote names Neil Young; PopMatters wrote in 2008 that For Emma, Forever Ago is the record where Justin Vernon "got away from touchstones like Tom Waits, Patty Griffin, Bob Dylan, Bruce Springsteen, and Neil Young," and the Journal Sentinel reported that his mother sang Indigo Girls and Neil Young while driving her kids around.
Phoebe Bridgers told Guitar.com in June 2020 that she drew on influences from Billie Eilish to Guided by Voices, Caroline Polachek, Mitski and Big Thief while making Punisher.
Elliott Smith named Big Star's Radio City among his five favorite folk albums in a feature for Far Out.
Elliott Smith named Television's Marquee Moon among his favorite albums in an NME interview in March 2000.

Benjamin Nugent's biography Elliott Smith and the Big Nothing (2009), quoted on Wikipedia's Fugazi page, recounts a friend recalling Smith becoming "really super-obsessed" with Built to Spill and Fugazi, and admiring Ian MacKaye intensely.
Benjamin Nugent's Elliott Smith and the Big Nothing (2009) recounts a friend recalling Smith becoming "really super-obsessed" with Built to Spill and Fugazi, and admiring Doug Martsch.
NPR reported that Phoebe Bridgers came to Elliott Smith's work after his death and has listened to Figure 8 more times than she can count.

Claire Cottrill took over her own Apple Music playlist in July 2021 and wrote per-song notes, describing Elliott Smith's "I Didn't Understand" as the most heartbreaking song she has ever heard, on a playlist framed around the songs she listened to most while making Sling.
The Forty-Five described Snail Mail's Lush as a throwback that "worshipped at the altar of Liz Phair and Fiona Apple."

Producer John Leckie has said that seeing Jeff Buckley in September 1994 made Thom Yorke realize falsetto singing was viable for him, and Travis's Dougie Payne has said Yorke's singing changed noticeably afterward; Wikipedia cites this account via Dalton's 1997 profile.
The New Yorker reported, per Far Out's paraphrase, that the revelation music could diverge from mainstream pop came to Mitski via Jeff Buckley, who introduced her to a different form of songwriting.

The Skinny reported that Mitski discovered Bjork at a listening station in a Japanese record store at age fifteen and was terrified -- it viscerally scared her; she has said Vespertine especially helped her look further into herself, and that she wasn't ready for it at fifteen, and that Bjork opened up a world of music and taught her there are a million ways to put sounds and thoughts together.
The same Guitar.com interview from June 2020 names Mitski among the influences Phoebe Bridgers drew on while making Punisher.

Sharon Van Etten told the Irish Times in August 2025 that she listened to "dandies of doom" as an angst-ridden adolescent, including the Cure, Joy Division and Nine Inch Nails, recalling shutting her bedroom door and upsetting her mother; Billboard reported in January 2025 that her Attachment Theory demos read as UK-influenced, citing Joy Division and Kate Bush.

When producer John Congleton asked Sharon Van Etten about her influences before Remind Me Tomorrow (2019), she named Nick Cave's Skeleton Tree; Stereogum separately put to her that Cave was a big influence on the record, which she didn't dispute. She has repeated the connection across at least six interviews, including Billboard.

Sharon Van Etten named Suicide in the same reference conversation with producer John Congleton before Remind Me Tomorrow (2019), a connection she has repeated across at least six interviews, including Billboard.

Sharon Van Etten named Portishead in the same reference conversation with producer John Congleton before Remind Me Tomorrow (2019), a connection she has repeated across at least six interviews, including Billboard.

Ethel Cain told The FADER in May 2022 that while making the record she was listening to slowcore and midwest emo acts like Title Fight and American Football, along with "female singers that are very lazy like Mazzy Star"; Nylon listed Mazzy Star's psychedelic melancholy among the album's ingredients that September.

Ethel Cain told Crack Magazine in a December 2022 cover story that friends she met on Tumblr as a teenager introduced her to artists who "influence her to this day," naming Daughter, Banks, Susanne Sundfor and Imogen Heap; she told Vice in July 2024 that discovering that side of pop made her think, "that's what I want to make."

Lindsey Jordan named Liz Phair in the same 2016 9:30 Club interview in which she named Grouper, Broadcast, Joni Mitchell, Psychic TV and Beat Happening as artists she was listening to while writing Habit.

Lindsey Jordan said in a 2016 interview at the 9:30 Club, posted to Tumblr, that while writing Habit she was listening to a lot of Grouper, Broadcast, Joni Mitchell, Psychic TV, Beat Happening and Liz Phair, adding that not all of them influenced the album stylistically but she had learned from their songwriting, which she called articulate and inspirational.
The same 2016 9:30 Club interview names Broadcast alongside Grouper, Joni Mitchell, Psychic TV, Beat Happening and Liz Phair as artists Lindsey Jordan was listening to while writing Habit.
Michelle Zauner told CBC's Q that seeing Karen O, a fellow half-Korean woman, on stage was a big reason she felt the courage to start playing music herself.

Claire Cottrill told Far Out that her influences are a mixture of her parents' tastes -- her father's soul records (Al Green, Brenton Wood, Billy Paul) and her mother's alternative music, including Cocteau Twins, Trashcan Sinatras, The The and PiL -- and that she falls somewhere between them; Apple Music's artist bio and Crack Magazine corroborate the Cocteau Twins connection.

Julia Holter played and discussed Cocteau Twins' "Fluffy Tufts" at a CalArts forum on her own musical influences in October 2015, alongside Joni Mitchell's Court and Spark, Bryan Ferry's vibrato and Ariel Pink.

Alan Sparhawk named Brian Eno and Joy Division as inspirations in a 1995 Billboard interview, alongside the boredom of living in Duluth -- quoted in Rolling Stone's obituary for Mimi Parker in November 2022.

Codeine predate and are widely cited as a formative reference point for the slowcore sound Low worked in; the same lineage claim recurs independently in Duster's and American Football's own accounts of what they were listening to.

Have a Nice Life have named Joy Division as an influence across three independent interviews: Todestrieb (2007), where Dan Barrett unprompted cited Xasthur and Lurker of Chalice for their bedroom-recording aesthetic "as well as older bands like My Bloody Valentine and Sisters of Mercy, Joy Division"; Last Day Deaf (2008), where Tim Macuga said he bought Unknown Pleasures as a teenager, with Barrett calling it a "huge influence, obviously"; and Steel for Brains, where Barrett named Sisters of Mercy, Joy Division and My Bloody Valentine as the bands influencing Have a Nice Life most directly, while noting they weren't childhood listening.

The same three interviews (Todestrieb 2007, Last Day Deaf 2008, Steel for Brains) in which Have a Nice Life named Joy Division also name My Bloody Valentine -- Tim Macuga has said he bought Loveless as a teenager soon after discovering Joy Division, with Dan Barrett calling both "huge influences, obviously."
Kurt Vile said in an interview with Under the Radar in April 2022 that he grew up listening to the Velvet Underground.

Dev Hynes describes writing "a song that did to Paul Westerberg what he did to Big Star" -- a compositional model rather than a statement of admiration.
Dev Hynes cites Massive Attack as his model for how Blood Orange is built -- the one-person-plus-rotating-guests format -- rather than as a sonic influence.

Natural Snow Buildings to OndaRock, naming their influences: "Kath Bloom and Loren Mazzacane Connors to Tarentel, Neil Young, Six Organs Of Admittance, Charalambides, Alice Coltrane, Stars Of The Lid, film scores, music from all parts of the world."

Kurt Cobain in Melody Maker (1992), on Pod: "The main reason I like them is for their songs, for the way they structure them, which is totally unique, very atmospheric." He also said "I wish Kim was allowed to write more songs for the Pixies, because 'Gigantic' is the best Pixies song, and Kim wrote it." Kim Deal has separately said she believes Nirvana hired Steve Albini for In Utero because of Pod.

Kim Deal to PopMatters: "I was listening to a lot of Harvest last year, now that you mention it. Because my Volvo only has a cassette player, so I listened to that tape constantly. And I was listening to that a lot when I was writing Fate to Fatal." What she was listening to while writing, so favourites tier rather than a shaping claim.

Dean Ween to Berklee Online, on the record collections he and Aaron Freeman grew up between: "Aaron's dad didn't have a lot of records either, but between the cool ones that I had and the cool ones he had, that's kind of what Ween is. He had everything from Nina Simone to the first two Velvet Underground records, to Richie Havens' Alarm Clock, to... everything, Beefheart."

rejectedEdges.citation: Ian MacKaye to Gothamist: "I remember in the beginning of Fugazi everyone was saying 'Oh clearly these guys have listened to a lot of Gang of Four.' But I had never listened to Gang of Four so it wasn't actually accurate." He adds that the songs being compared were his own, written before Guy Picciotto began contributing: "Guy was a fan of Gang of Four but the stuff people were comparing to Gang of Four was written by me before Guy started contributing compositions." Logged contested rather than clean precisely because MacKaye confirms Picciotto's fandom -- the denial covers the songs at issue and MacKaye's own listening, not every member.
Paul Banks/Interpol guitarist Daniel Kessler has denied the comparison across 2002, 2007 and 2012 interviews: "It has absolutely nothing to do with me. I don't know where that shit comes from."
The only documented connection is that Steve Shelley drummed on Cat Power's first two albums -- personnel, not a stated influence.
Tom Verlaine resisted the comparison across numerous interviews, naming Albert Ayler and John Coltrane as his real touchstones instead.
Nick Zinner has rejected the comparison; the only positive evidence found for it was an editorially-curated Apple Music playlist, not an artist statement.

Natalie Mering has said she has always liked Nico but could never fully relate to her, unable to relate to her life and feeling Nico had the advantage of being extremely beautiful -- admiration paired with an explicit reservation.
Producer Brad Wood has said Liz Phair's chord shapes "have more to do with like, Glenn Branca than Joni Mitchell" -- an insider contradicting a comparison Phair herself hasn't addressed.
Mark E. Smith called David Bowie "crap," grouping him with Genesis, Pink Floyd and James Taylor.
MOJO reported that Mark E. Smith visibly shivers at the comparison to Bob Dylan.
Tommy Ramone's Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction remarks explicitly separated the band's CBGB-era peers, including Television, from the artists who actually influenced them.
The same Rock and Roll Hall of Fame remarks in which Tommy Ramone separated Television from the band's influences apply equally to Talking Heads, another CBGB-era peer rather than a stated influence.

Far Out Magazine, asked whether Swans' live cover of "Love Will Tear Us Apart" was a tribute to Ian Curtis, Michael Gira dispelled the argument that he is in any way indebted to the Joy Division frontman.

Louder Than War (2014), Andrew Savage by email: says Pavement isn't a big influence and that Parquet Courts share similar influences instead, naming the Velvet Underground, Roxy Music and the Fall. Malkmus's remark about mistaking a Parquet Courts song for his own band is a third-party comparison; Savage's response in Hot Press is bemusement.

NOW Magazine (2016), Will Toledo asked directly: he grew up on the Beatles, the Who, the Kinks and the Beach Boys, explicitly not Pavement, Sonic Youth or Dinosaur Jr, attributing the resemblance to those bands having listened to the same older music he did.
Same NOW Magazine (2016) quote as the Pavement denial -- Toledo names the Beatles, the Who, the Kinks and the Beach Boys as his actual upbringing, explicitly not Sonic Youth.

Westword: a "pet peeve" Toledo says he's heard since 2011; he never really listened to the Strokes -- a commonality of influence, not descent.

INDY Week interview: the interviewer proposes Prefab Sprout, Thomas Dolby and Gary Numan as reference points for ken; Dan Bejar redirects to something more basic -- New Order, the Cure, Echo & the Bunnymen. The Numan framing came from the interviewer's question, not Bejar's answer.

Westword (2010), asked about Tori Amos/Kate Bush comparisons: Annie Clark says she loves Kate Bush but doesn't feel she's carrying on her tradition, and was "probably more influenced by Stravinsky" on that record -- then discusses "Wuthering Heights" admiringly and technically (the harmony, the bar of fifths in the chorus) as a valuable lesson. Georgia Straight's fourteen-year retrospective does list Kate Bush among her invaluable influences. Admiration and technical study alongside an explicit refusal of the lineage framing. Recorded for its own sake -- kate-bush isn't a graph node.
Matt Berninger's much-quoted line: the Strokes influenced more bands in ten years than the artists he named did in twenty-five -- a claim about their importance, not his own descent.

Berninger calls Arcade Fire "hugely influential to aspiring musicians" with a direct connection to people's hearts -- a compliment about their reach, not a stated influence on The National; also chronologically awkward.

Westword: asked whether the Chameleons, Comsat Angels and the Sound informed Interpol's sound alongside Joy Division, Paul Banks said he'd never heard any of those bands before starting Interpol, and has only heard the Chameleons since the band put out records.

Louder Than War: Mark Burgess says he saw Joy Division live five or six times and found them "a bit of a mess early on" without feeling musically influenced by them, though he took notice once Closer came out, calling it "on a different level."
Rolling Stone, "The Cranberries: The Hidden Power of Dreams": Noel Hogan says "If we do sound like other bands, like the Sundays, then that's coincidence."

Labrador Records interview: Johan Duncanson, asked about the constant My Bloody Valentine/Jesus and Mary Chain comparisons, dismissed the latter directly -- "jamc is a boring and very heterosexual rock band that wrote a few good songs" -- while affirming a genuine appreciation for My Bloody Valentine in the same breath.

The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: Mike Hadreas says he'd never heard Talk Talk until fans compared his third album, Too Bright, to them, and only listened afterward -- discovery following the comparison, not preceding the work it's supposedly informing.

A Fall 2006 Q&A archived at content.jasonmolina.org: asked about Leonard Cohen comparisons, Jason Molina said he "didn't hear a single song I know of by Leonard Cohen until I was about out of college, so it would be hard to call him a regular influence."

Victoria Legrand to Drowned In Sound (Nov 2007): "I personally don't hear the ostentatious similarity with our music and the Cocteau Twins." Alex Scally, separately: "We didn't really listen to them. Strangely, they weren't part of us." Contested rather than clean because an unverified later report has Legrand professing admiration for the band -- but a favourites statement is a weaker claim than a shaping influence two members explicitly reject.

Kurt Cobain to Jon Savage (New York, 22 July 1993), asked directly about his influences: "I stayed away from Joy Division. I've heard a few of their songs and I know I would really like it, but just the mystique about it and the stories I've heard, I know that's the band to listen to, of all of them. I'm just waiting." The handwritten top-50 album list in his Journals carries no Joy Division entry either.

Isaac Brock to The Rocket (summer 1997): "I'm scared to death of becoming a band like Pavement" -- they "put out a really amazing album, Slanted and Enchanted, that had a really great feeling, and somewhere they lost it. They got overproduced." Contested rather than clean because he praises the record in the same breath; what he rejects is Pavement as a model, not their existence in his listening.
